stem: Around 185 BCE, the last Maurya emperor was assassinated by his commander-in-chief. Who was he?
options: Kharavela of Kalinga
Pushyamitra Shunga
Gautamiputra Satakarni
Karikala of the Cholas
explanation: Correct option: (B). Pushyamitra Shunga, the commander-in-chief, assassinated the last Maurya emperor around 185 BCE and founded the Shunga dynasty. Kharavela was a Chedi king of Kalinga, Gautamiputra Satakarni was a Satavahana ruler and Karikala was a Chola king; none of them ended Maurya rule.

stem: Why do some scholars call the period after the Maurya empire the 'age of reorganisation'?
options: Regions were reorganised into new kingdoms competing for power
The Mauryas reorganised their provinces into smaller districts
One foreign ruler reorganised all regions into a single empire
Kingdoms stopped competing and reorganised trade with each other
explanation: Correct option: (A). After the Maurya empire broke up, existing regions were reorganised into new kingdoms that constantly competed to become powerful, and the map of India changed greatly. The Mauryas were no longer in power, no single ruler united all regions, and the kingdoms did not stop competing.

stem: A king arranges the marriage of his daughter into the royal family of a neighbouring kingdom so that the two kingdoms become allies. This is an example of:
options: a tributary arrangement
an ashvamedha yajna
a matrimonial alliance
a council of ascetics
explanation: Correct option: (C). A matrimonial alliance is an alliance arranged through a marriage between members of two royal families, often to cement friendship between kingdoms; it was a peaceful way of gaining control. A tributary kingdom pays tribute to an overlord, the ashvamedha yajna was a Vedic ritual to claim supremacy, and a council of ascetics was a gathering of sages created by Kharavela.

stem: A student makes a timeline from the first year of the 2nd century BCE (200 BCE) to the last year of the 3rd century CE (300 CE). How many years does it cover? (There is no year zero.)
options: 100 years
300 years
400 years
500 years
explanation: Correct option: (D). From 200 BCE to 1 BCE there are 200 years, and from 1 CE to 300 CE there are 300 years, so the period covers 200 + 300 = 500 years. 100 years comes from subtracting 200 from 300, which is wrong because BCE years count backwards; 300 and 400 years leave out one of the two parts of the timeline.

stem: Many kingdoms that emerged after the Maurya empire broke up had earlier been tributary kingdoms under Maurya overlordship. What does this most reasonably suggest?
options: Regional powers already existed and asserted themselves once the overlord fell
The Mauryas had ruled every village directly, leaving no local rulers behind
All of the new kingdoms were founded by invaders from outside the subcontinent
Tributary kingdoms were created only after the death of the last Maurya emperor
explanation: Correct option: (A). Tributary kingdoms had their own rulers who accepted Maurya overlordship; when the empire broke up, these regional powers became independent kingdoms. If the Mauryas had ruled every village directly, there would have been no tributary kingdoms. Most of the new dynasties, such as the Shungas, Satavahanas and Chedis, were from within the subcontinent, and the tributary kingdoms existed before, not after, the empire's end.

stem: During an ashvamedha yajna, the king's horse wanders into a neighbouring territory and its ruler stops the horse. According to the custom, what would follow?
options: The horse would be sent back and the ritual would end
The territory would join the empire without any dispute
The king would pay tribute to the ruler who stopped it
A battle would be fought to decide which ruler was supreme
explanation: Correct option: (D). stem: The Bharhut Stupa was probably built in Ashoka's time. What did the Shungas contribute to it?
options: Carved railings and reliefs showing stories from the Buddha's life
A pillar inscription praising Vasudeva as the god of gods
Rock-cut rooms for Jain monks with a record of the king's deeds
Red sandstone statues of Kubera with prominent moustaches
explanation: Correct option: (A). The Shungas added beautifully carved railings and reliefs depicting stories from the Buddha's life to the Bharhut Stupa, among the earliest examples of Buddhist art. The pillar praising Vasudeva is the Heliodorus pillar, the rock-cut Jain caves with an inscription are at Udayagiri near Bhubaneswar, and red sandstone Kubera figures belong to the Mathura school.

stem: The Shunga period saw a revival of Vedic rituals, yet the Shungas also added Buddhist reliefs to the Bharhut Stupa. Which conclusion is best supported by this?

Other schools of thought still flourished alongside Vedic practices
Buddhist art at Bharhut was made only by foreign Greek craftsmen

stem: Why are the Udayagiri-Khandagiri caves near Bhubaneswar considered notable examples of 'rock-cut architecture'?

Their rooms, panels and statues were carved out of the rock
Their halls were made from wooden beams joined together

explanation: Correct option: (B). stem: The Chola king Karikala built the Kallanai or Grand Anicut on the Kaveri. How did it help the region earn the name 'rice bowl of the South'?

It allowed large ships to sail upstream to the Chola capital
It protected the Chola kingdom from Chera and Pandya attacks

stem: Megasthenes described the Pandya kingdom as trading with distant powers like the Greeks and Romans, and Kharavela stated that he had hundreds of pearls brought from the Pandya kingdom. What do these two sources together show?

The Pandyas traded only with foreign powers across the sea

stem: Which statement best evaluates the cultural life of the age of reorganisation as described in the chapter?
options: Foreign styles replaced Indian themes in art and literature
Each kingdom developed its culture in complete isolation
Constant wars brought art and literature to a standstill
Cultures blended, but Indian themes remained dominant
explanation: Correct option: (D).
